[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments comparing fixed-bottleneck architectures (e.g., VAE with constant latent size) against dynamic expansion methods (e.g., progressive networks, dynamically expandable networks) on split-MNIST and permuted-MNIST continual learning benchmarks — Directly tests whether a fixed bottleneck fails to reallocate resources, by measuring task-specific forgetting (stability) and learning speed (plasticity) across tasks. If dynamic methods outperform fixed bottlenecks on these metrics, the hypothesis is supported; if not, it may be refuted.

[PATH:theoretical] Literature review and theoretical analysis of information bottleneck theory applied to continual learning (e.g., papers by Tishby, Achille, or recent works on representational capacity trade-offs) — Provides a principled framework to understand whether a fixed bottleneck imposes a fundamental bound on the stability-plasticity trade-off, independent of architecture specifics. Formal proofs or counterexamples from this literature can confirm or refute the claim that resource reallocation is necessary.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical study of adaptive bottleneck mechanisms (e.g., attention-based gating, mixture-of-experts with learned routing) in continual learning settings, measuring representational overlap and task-specific neuron utilization via techniques like activation maximization or representational similarity analysis — Directly examines the role of dynamic reallocation by comparing fixed bottlenecks to architectures that can shift resources. If adaptive mechanisms show improved trade-off, the hypothesis is supported; if fixed bottlenecks can match performance via better regularization or rehearsal, it may be refuted.
